findings.summary: Page 2 prescribes the `${f@Q}` ssh remedy before page 4 explains that an ssh command line is parsed a second time on the remote host.
findings.evidence: Page 2 ends with `ssh host "rm -- ${f@Q}"   # safe` / `printf -v q %q "$f"       # pre-4.4`, note "quote once per extra parse"; the rationale arrives only on page 4: "The remote shell sees the text after local quote removal."
findings.fix: Move that entire code block from page 2 to page 4's "Remote Re-Parsing" section, so page 2's filename section ends on the `-print0` / `xargs -0` bullets and the ssh topic is taught once, in one place.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: The boundary table tells readers to send an array over ssh as `${cmd@Q}`, which expands only element 0 and silently drops every remaining argument.
findings.evidence: Code block on the same page defines cmd as an array — `ssh host "${cmd[*]@Q}"  # cmd is an array` — but the table row reads: ["`ssh host`","`${cmd@Q}`"]. For `cmd=(rsync -a src dst)`, `${cmd@Q}` is `${cmd[0]@Q}` = `'rsync'`.
findings.fix: Change the table cell to `${cmd[*]@Q}` (matching the code block), or add "(string)" / "`[*]@Q` for an array" so the bare `${cmd@Q}` form is not read as array-safe.

findings.summary: The two `ssh ... @Q` lines are taught under the "Status Traps" heading, above the "Remote Re-Parsing" heading that explains why they are needed.
findings.evidence: Under `{"type":"heading","text":"Status Traps"}` the code block begins `ssh host "grep ${pat@Q} /log"  # quote each arg` and `ssh host "${cmd[*]@Q}"  # cmd is an array`; only two blocks later does the heading "Remote Re-Parsing" explain "`ssh host \"$cmd\"` parses ==twice==: local, then remote."
findings.fix: Cut the two `ssh` lines from the "Status Traps" code block (leaving `export VAR=$(cmd)` and `VAR=$(cmd) || exit`) and re-place them as the code example under the "Remote Re-Parsing" heading, after the bullets that describe the double parse.

findings.summary: `set --` is described as the re-parse idiom for `getopts`, conflating the builtin `getopts` with the external `getopt`.
findings.evidence: "`set --` is the standard re-parse trick after `getopts`." The standard idiom after the `getopts` builtin is `shift $((OPTIND-1))`; `set --` re-parsing belongs to the external `getopt`, as in `eval set -- "$(getopt -o ab: -- "$@")"`.
findings.fix: Split the claim: "`shift $((OPTIND-1))` after `getopts`; `eval set -- \"$(getopt ...)\"` for the external `getopt`."

findings.summary: The page calls numeric contexts "the one quote-free zone" and then lists four quote-free contexts in the table directly below it.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Numeric contexts are the one quote-free zone: `$(( ))` and subscripts." Table "The Four Exceptions": `[[ ]]` `(( ))`, `x=$y`, `arr=($s)`, glob pattern.
findings.fix: Reword the bullet to "Numeric contexts never split or glob: `$(( ))` and array subscripts" so it stops claiming uniqueness and stops contradicting the four-exception table.

findings.summary: The bullet "Nor for any command whose status is tested" continues a negative claim that the preceding bullets no longer make.
findings.evidence: The list reads "`set -e` **does** fire on `x=$(cmd)`: it takes the substitution's status." … then "Nor for any command whose status is tested."
findings.fix: Rewrite the bullet as a standalone statement, e.g. "`set -e` also does not fire for any command whose status is tested (`if`, `&&`, `||`, `!`)."

findings.summary: The claim that xtrace quoting is a Bash 4.4+ feature is wrong by more than a decade — set -x has quoted its trace since Bash 2.x.
findings.evidence: "`set -x` traces after expansion; Bash 4.4+ quotes the trace." Bash NEWS (2.x section): "The trace output (set -x) now inserts quotes where necessary so it can be reused as input."
findings.fix: Drop the version gate: "`set -x` traces after expansion, and quotes the trace so boundaries are visible." If a version is wanted, cite Bash 2.x, not 4.4 (4.4 is the right version for `${var@Q}`, `mapfile -d`, and `inherit_errexit`, which the deck already uses correctly).

findings.evidence: Page 6: "`set -e` still has the holes from the gotchas page." Page 2 ("Where Missing Quotes Bite") never mentions `set -e`; the holes appear on page 5: "A ==builtin prefix== … masks it." / "Without `shopt -s inherit_errexit`, a failure __inside__ is not caught".
findings.fix: Reword to "`set -e` still has the holes from the seven-rules page", or move the four `set -e` bullets from page 5 to page 2 so the reference resolves.
